deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts. Part A, the top half, is astronomy: general precession in equatorial and ecliptic coordinates, continuing the previous page. Part B, the bottom half, is arithmetic in the Gaussian integers Z[i]: integer parts of (a+bi)(5±2i)/7 over a small system of residues mod 7.

PART A. PRECESSION.

(A1) Small rotation formulas. The top lines are labelled with words I cannot read securely ('Hülfs?'/'Polst?'):
- dδ/dt = k cos α
- dα/dt = −k sin α tan δ
These give the change of α and δ under an infinitesimal rotation of the sphere by k about the equatorial axis through α = 90°/270°. Recall the previous page's convention: x = sin α cos δ, y = cos α cos δ, z = sin δ. The ecliptic pole lies at α = 270°, δ = 90° − ε. So a lunisolar rotation Δ about the ecliptic pole splits into:
- Δ cos ε about the equatorial pole;
- Δ sin ε about that equatorial axis.
Hence k = Δ sin ε, up to a sign convention. The sign of the α-term here is opposite to the line below; that is a convention change, not an error.

(A2) Constants. Gauss sets Δ = 50.238″, the annual lunisolar precession along the ecliptic. He introduces p, the planetary precession: the annual shift of the equinox along the equator. The annual precession in right ascension and declination is then:
- dα = 45.8817″ + 20.0059″ sin α tan δ = Δ cos ε − p + Δ sin ε sin α tan δ
- dδ = 20.0059″ cos α = Δ sin ε cos α
He also records log10 20.0059 = 1.3011582.
The implied values (my computation):
- With ε ≈ 23°27′55″, Δ sin ε = 20.006, so n = 20.0059″ fits.
- Δ cos ε = 46.083″, so p = 46.083 − 45.8817 ≈ 0.20″.
These are the classical m and n of the precession: m = ψ cos ε − χ, n = ψ sin ε.

(A3) Cartesian form, with x = cos δ sin α, y = cos δ cos α, z = sin δ:
- dx = yΔ cos ε − yp
- dy = −xΔ cos ε + xp − Δ z sin ε
- dz = Δ y sin ε
These follow from the previous page's relations dx = y dα − sin α · z dδ, dy = −x dα − cos α · z dδ, dz = cos δ dδ. Substituting dα and dδ from (A2), the sin ε terms cancel in dx and combine in dy. I have verified this.

(A4) Ecliptic Cartesian coordinates, ξ = cos b sin λ, η = cos b cos λ, ζ = sin b, with ξ = x cos ε + z sin ε, η = y, ζ = −x sin ε + z cos ε. Lunisolar precession Δ is a rotation about the ecliptic pole. The p-term is a rotation about the equatorial pole: in equatorial coordinates dx = −yp, dy = xp. Hence:
- dξ = Δη − ηp cos ε
- dη = −Δξ + p(ξ cos ε − ζ sin ε)
- dζ = ηp sin ε
In dη the bracket equals x, so that term is just px.

(A5) Longitude and latitude. From dλ = (η dξ − ξ dη)/cos²b:
- dλ = Δ − p cos ε + p sin ε sin λ tan b = 50.054″ + 0.08″ sin λ tan b
- Check: 50.238 − 0.2011 × 0.9173 = 50.0535, and p sin ε = 0.080.
The line '∂b =' is left blank. My completion: db = dζ / cos b = p sin ε cos λ ≈ 0.08″ cos λ.

Purpose: tabulating annual precession for star reductions in equatorial and ecliptic coordinates. The p-part is modelled as a rotation of the frame about the equatorial pole. This is exactly right for α and δ. For λ and b it is only a simplified model of the ecliptic's motion: the true effect is a rotation of the ecliptic about its node line, π sin(λ − Π) type terms, with an obliquity change. Gauss's 0.08″ sin λ tan b term is therefore a model-dependent approximation.

PART B. GAUSSIAN INTEGERS MOD 7; heading '7 et 39', probably '7 et 29' since N(5+2i) = 29.

(B1) Products. Gauss forms the products of 5+2i with the elements a+bi, a = 1..3 (sometimes 4), b = 0..3. A dot diagram with a drawn rectangle shows this block of lattice points. The products he lists are:
- 0+i → −2+5i
- 1+i → 3+7i
- 1+2i → 1+12i
- 2+2i → 6+14i
- 1+3i → −1+17i; 2+3i → 4+19i; 3+3i → 9+21i; 4+3i → 14+23i
Successive entries differ by 5+2i.

(B2) Integer parts with 5+2i. For each a+bi he takes the Gaussian integer part, real and imaginary floors, of (a+bi)(5+2i)/7. His table:

| a+bi | 1 | 2 | 3 | 1+i | 2+i | 3+i | 1+2i | 2+2i | 3+2i | 1+3i | 2+3i | 3+3i |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| floor | 0 | 1 | 2 | i | 1+i | 1+i | i | 2i | 1+2i | −1+2i | 2i | 1+3i |

All entries check.

(B3) The same with 5−2i. Products: 7+3i, 12+i, 17−i; 9+8i, 14+6i, 19+4i; 11+13i, 16+11i, 21+9i. Integer parts of (a+bi)(5−2i)/7:

| a+bi | 1 | 2 | 3 | 1+i | 2+i | 3+i | 1+2i | 2+2i | 3+2i | 1+3i | 2+3i | 3+3i |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| floor | −i | 1−i | 2−i | 1 | 1 | 2−i | 1+i | 2 | 2 | 1+i | 2+i | 3+i |

All entries check.

(B4) Other jottings:
- '1|4, 2|8, 3|12' is k → 4k.
- The column 3−3i, 4−i, 5+i, 6+3i is an arithmetic progression with step 1+2i.
- The column 3, 2+2i, 1+5i(?), 0+7i, 6+14i, 18 and the scratch '5+2i · 6+2i: 30, 4, …' are unclear. The true product is (5+2i)(6+2i) = 26+22i.

Interpretation (my inference): this is the Z[i] analogue of the floor-function / lattice-point counting used in Gauss's lemma and his third proof of quadratic reciprocity, for the inert prime 7 and the prime 5±2i of norm 29. It looks like an experiment toward biquadratic residues and reciprocity. The page header suggests 1810.
errors: In dη the transcription/handwriting shows '+xp(ξcosε − ζsinε)'. Correct is +p(ξcosε − ζsinε), which equals +px; the extra x would be a slip, or a misreading of the transcription.
The sign convention for the k-term at the top (−k sin α tan δ) is opposite to the later +Δ sin ε sin α tan δ. This is harmless: k = −Δ sin ε under the other orientation.
∂b is left blank. Under Gauss's model it should be p sin ε cos λ ≈ 0.08″ cos λ.

Modelling the planetary precession as a rotation about the equatorial pole gives the correct α and δ terms. For λ and b it is not the physical motion of the ecliptic, which is a rotation about the ecliptic node line with rate π. The sin λ tan b term is therefore a simplification.
The scratch computation '5+2i·6+2i = 30, 4, …' is incomplete or unclear; the true product is 26+22i.

deep.surprise_reason: The precession material is routine. The Z[i] floor-function tables show Gauss experimenting around 1810 with a Gaussian analogue of the lattice-point form of his lemma for an inert prime (7) and 5±2i. Gauss's early work on biquadratic residues (Tagebuch, Nachlass) is known, and similar fragments appear in Werke II. So this is a notable dated worked example rather than a new result.

transcription_corrections: In ∂η the term should read '+p(ξcosε − ζsinε)' (= +px), not 'xp(...)'.
The heading '7 et 39' may well be '7 et 29' (norm of 5±2i); page renumbering 39→27 makes the reading uncertain.
Entries like '−2+5', '3+7', '6 14', '4 19' are Gaussian integers −2+5i, 3+7i, 6+14i, 4+19i, etc.
In the 5−2i table, '1|0−1' means 1 → 0−i; '2−' in the 2+2i column should be '2'.
The top labels 'Halst'/'pist' are illegible words; the formulas are the effect of a rotation k about the equatorial axis at α=90°: dδ = k cosα, dα = −k sinα tanδ.
'b' in the ecliptic formulas is Gauss's Fraktur 𝔟 (ecliptic latitude).
